Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

swear verb

take an oath

also swear an oath, take an oath, oath, on oath, under oath, sworn, swear to

classical

Caes. B.C. 3.13: jūrat sē eum nōn dēsertūrum (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Off. 3.108: falsum jūrāre, to swear falsely (Lewis & Short)

jūrō, jūrāre, jūrāvī, jūrātum

verb, first conjugation · Conjugation on Wiktionary

swear, take an oath

What one swears follows in the accusative and infinitive. Jūrātus, having sworn, is “on oath”; injūrātus, “unsworn” (Plaut. Am. 281).

Other words

  • jūs jūrandum, jūris jūrandī n. — an oath

    also used · classical · Cic. Off. 3.104: est enim jūs jūrandum affirmātiō religiōsa (Lewis & Short); Liv. 21.1.4: jūre jūrandō adāctum

    Also written as one word. Jūs jūrandum dare, to give one’s oath; jūs jūrandum adigere aliquem (Caes. B.C. 1.76) and jūre jūrandō adigere (Liv. 21.1.4), to make someone swear; jūs jūrandum cōnservāre, to keep it (Cic. Off. 3.100).

  • dējerō, dējerāre, dējerāvī, dējerātum — swear solemnly, swear by the gods

    verb, first conjugation · also used · classical · Plaut. Cas. 3.5.37: per omnēs deōs et deās dējerāvit (Lewis & Short); Ter. Eun. 2.3.39 (Lewis & Short) · Conjugation on Wiktionary

    (vōx cōmica: Plaut., Ter.; later Gell.)

    Morgan–Owens, after Vives, gives it for swearing in the sense of bad language; classically it is only taking an oath (Lewis & Short). For swearing at someone, see abuse.

Examples

  • altāribus admōtum tāctīs sacrīs jūre jūrandō adāctum sē cum prīmum posset hostem fore populō Rōmānō

    brought to the altar, his hand on the offerings, he was made to swear that as soon as he could he would be an enemy of RomeLiv. 21.1.4

See also by Hercules!, promise, abuse.

SourcesLewis & Short: juro · Lewis & Short: jusjurandum · Lewis & Short: dejero
